transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2028-09-12 15:00 PT
Duration: 57 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Maya Torres (Redwood Product), Lena Ortiz (Pyxis Head of ML), Marcus Ng (Pyxis Platform Eng), Priya Shah (CTO), Daniel Rios (SRE)
Links shared: Console demo deck (slides.redwood/optimize-demo), cost model spreadsheet (drive.redwood/pyxis-costs), quickstart repo (github.redwood/pyxis-sample)

Summary: Quick walkthrough of Redwood Optimize console features — batching, prefix/KV cache recommendations, and cost-model scenarios. Ran through three live scenarios with Pyxis representative traffic to show cost tradeoffs. Discussed private deployment concerns (VPC, KMS) and agreed to a short pilot bench to validate numbers.

Topics: cost models, batching strategy, prefix vs session cache, KV prefetch lookahead, latency SLOs, dedicated vs hosted, compliance requirements (SOC2/KMS), pilot plan

Transcript:
[00:00] Samira: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off, i'm samira from redwood, i'll run the high level and ethan will dive into the console and the cost sim, quick intro around objectives — 45 minute walkthrough, 10 minute q&a, sound good?
[00:18] Lena: yeah that works, thanks. we mainly want to understand where we can get steady unit-cost wins without blowing our p95 latency, and what tradeoffs you recommend for our use case (low-latency chat assistant + nightly batch embeddings).
[00:30] Ethan: perfect. Marcus — do you still have the qps shape you sent over? we'll reference it in the scenarios.
[00:36] Marcus: yep uploaded to the sheet, it's the production-peak-aug.csv. peak is roughly 480 rps with a long tail and lots of short sessions.
[00:45] Ethan: nice, that's helpful. ok first slide is a one-line summary of optimize: console suggests batching and caching profiles, runs cost sims on your actual traffic, and recommends kernel/quantization and prefetch settings.
[01:12] Jordan: just to flag, some of the auto names in the deck are wonky — the export might show KV as K-V or K V in some transcripts, so apologies if we have a mismatch with your internal terms.
[01:25] Priya: no problem, we've seen that with other tools too.
[01:30] Ethan: jumping in, here's the console demo. we'll load the pyxis traffic trace — you can see request size distribution, session length, and expec token counts. from that we run three sims: conservative (low batching, low prefetch), balanced (moderate batch + prefix cache), and aggressive (high batch, larger prefetch window).
[01:58] [screen share noise]
[02:05] Ethan: scenario A — conservative: target p95 < 300ms, batch size cap 4, prefetch disabled, session cache only. cost per 1M tokens baseline here is $X (spreadsheet inserts real numbers), latency meets SLO but unit cost is higher.
[02:30] Lena: can you explain session cache vs prefix cache here? we've used sessionization in our own infra but haven't done prefix kv lookahead.
[02:38] Ethan: sure — session cache stores KV for active sessions only, good when you have few, long-lived sessions. prefix/KV lookahead caches common prompt prefixes across sessions which helps with high fan-out and many short sessions. it can reduce per-token compute since the KV doesn't need recomputation for common prefixes. downside is memory footprint and more cache lookup churn.
[03:05] Marcus: in our traffic we have lots of short sessions with repeated system messages and similar user prompts, so prefix cache sounds promising. what's the memory delta?
[03:14] Jordan: in our runtime a prefix cache with a 3-5 turn lookahead increased GPU memory by ~6-12% depending on model family; we show that in the model-profile tab of the sheet.
[03:27] Ethan: right. scenario B — balanced: we enable prefix caching for the top 12% of prefixes as ranked by access frequency, set adaptive batching (up to 24 tokens), and keep concurrency soft limits to preserve p95. cost per 1M tokens drops ~28% in the sim for your traces. this is the recommended starting point.
[03:55] Priya: 28% is big. does that assume quantization or lower-accuracy kernels? we need to preserve quality.
[04:03] Ethan: good call. the sim here holds model variant constant — same FP16 precision. optimize will recommend quantization only if it passes the quality gate for your eval prompts. quality monitoring is part of the pipeline — we tie regressions back to prompt sets.
[04:22] Lena: and the quality gate — is that manual or automated? can we hook in our own eval suite?
[04:28] Ethan: both. you can use the console to define evals, and Optimize will run A/B and regression checks when it suggests quant or larger prefetch windows. we won't auto-apply quant changes without approval.
[04:45] Daniel: how does lookahead work with streaming responses? we stream tokens to clients and don't want added latency.
[04:52] Jordan: prefix caching is orthogonal to streaming — the runtime can serve cached KV for the prefix and then resume streaming new tokens with no additional fetches. worst case there's tiny microsecond synch on cache lookup, but we keep that sub-ms in production. the bigger latencies come from batching waiting for more requests.
[05:14] Marcus: so batching adds queuing delay; how do we see the latency vs cost tradeoff in the console?
[05:20] Ethan: console shows a latency budget slider — you can set an acceptable p50/p95 increase and it will search for batching sizing/concurrency that maximizes savings under that constraint. you get a Sim Results table with expected cost, expected p95, and hit-rate for prefix cache.
[05:42] Priya: can you run one of the sims live with our trace?
[05:45] Ethan: sure, running scenario B live now — give me a few seconds to apply the trace.
[06:05] [ambient typing]
[06:12] Ethan: ok sim ran. results: balanced config yields estimated 26–31% savings depending on burst smoothing assumptions — sheet shows the three columns. p95 moves from 210ms baseline to 240ms in the balanced sim — still within your 300ms target.
[06:35] Lena: that's acceptable. how confident are you in the sim? do you run micro-benchmarks or is it purely analytic?
[06:41] Ethan: it's hybrid. we combine measured kernel throughput (collected per model/hardware profile), observed token-rate distributions from your trace, and queueing models. we also recommend running a short bench on dedicated instances to validate— hence the pilot.
[06:58] Samira: we generally see the sim accuracy within ~5–12% of bench runs for similar workloads, caveats for high variance tail traffic.
[07:08] Marcus: ok, pilot makes sense. what about routing — can we route production-critical users to dedicated pools and non-critical to hosted variants?
[07:18] Jordan: yes, smart routing supports model variants and pool tiers. you can route by token type, customer id, or header. fallback policies exist if dedicated pool saturates.
[07:28] Priya: on compliance — SOC2, KMS, and audit logs — do you support customer-managed keys and VPC-only control plane?
[07:36] Samira: yes, for Private deployments we support customer KMS/HSM integration, VPC peering, and long-term audit retention options. we'll send the SOC2 report and the private deployment checklist.
[07:49] Lena: do you support on-prem GPU clusters? we have a data residency constraint for EU customers.
[07:56] Ethan: we have a private on-prem package. it requires an ops install and we help with the initial sizing; note that some of the autoscaling features are constrained by your environment but core runtime, cache, and batching logic are identical.
[08:12] Priya: good. what about cost for dedicated pools vs hosted? our finance team will ask about committed vs usage.
[08:19] Samira: committed reserved capacity is monthly or annual; we can model break-evens in the spreadsheet. generally if you have consistent baseline usage above ~X GPU-hours/week, Dedicated tends to be more economical and gives lower variance in latency.
[08:36] Marcus: one thing — our sessions have a lot of repeated system messages; that's low-entropy but varies per tenant. how do you handle tenant boundaries in prefix cache? we don't want cross-tenant leakage.
[08:49] Ethan: prefix cache respects tenancy keys; cached entries are namespaced by tenant id. we also support TTLs and eviction policies per-namespace. we can show a sandbox where we set tenant-specific TTL=12 hours and max-entries 200k and simulate cache hit rates.
[09:07] Lena: show us the hit-rate numbers for top 10% prefixes?
[09:11] [screen flicker]
[09:15] Ethan: here — for your trace, top 10% prefixes account for ~42% of prefix lookups; hit rate for the balanced config is 36% effective reduced compute because of partial misses.
[09:28] Priya: can we prewarm the prefix cache from our historical logs instead of learning over time?
[09:34] Jordan: yes, you can seed the KV store with known prefixes, we provide a loader script (sample in repo) and you can bucketize keys to avoid hot-spotting. that's often useful during an initial rollout.
[09:46] Marcus: about memory — you said ~6-12% for small lookahead, does that scale linearly? if we double lookahead window does memory scale 2x?
[09:55] Jordan: roughly linear, yes — because each additional token step increases KV size, but deduplication across prefixes reduces growth. the sheet includes a memory delta curve per model.
[10:08] Lena: let's talk about noisy bursts — holidays cause 6x spikes for us. does Optimize propose burst capacity or fallback policies to preserve availability?
[10:17] Ethan: console suggests burst policies — maintain a small reserved burst pool and degrade gracefully: prioritize system prompts, apply aggressive batching for non-critical routes, and use cheaper model variants for long-run generations. fallback policy is configurable per-route.
[10:32] Priya: are those fallbacks automatic? we need to review business logic before degrading.
[10:36] Ethan: fallbacks are opt-in; we can simulate policy effects in the sim. they are applied only when thresholds hit and can notify SRE channels.
[10:45] Samira: quick note — competitors like Anthropic and Bedrock focus on model access; they don't bundle the same runtime-driven cost tooling. Replicate has lightweight routing but not enterprise KV prefetch sim like Optimize.
[10:59] Marcus: makes sense. ok, can you walk through what we'd need to do to start the pilot?
[11:06] Ethan: pilot plan — we provision a sandbox tenant, ingest 1–2 hours of your traces, run bench with comparable instance types (we'll match your preferred GPU family), and give a results deck. we'll set up monitoring hooks so you can push alerts to slack/datadog.
[11:22] Lena: timeline? we want results in two weeks.
[11:25] Samira: doable — samira: we'll target bench kick-off 9/15, bench completes by 9/18, review on 9/19.
[11:33] Priya: agree. please email the requirements for traces and any VPN/peering work.
[11:38] Samira: will do.
[11:40] Daniel: small question — how are costs reported back? itemized per-token, per-route, and GPU-hour?
[11:46] Jordan: we provide token-level breakdowns, per-route cost, model variant cost, and infra GPU-hours. console also has a waterfall that attributes savings to caching vs batching vs quantization.
[11:57] Lena: great. technical nit — what's the KV TTL logic for multilingual prompts? we have prompts in EN + JP and keys might not be shared.
[12:05] Ethan: KV keys are prefix-hashed including normalized prompt text; if you normalize by language we can keep separate namespaces. often multilingual reduces hit rates, but you can tune prefetched prefix sets per-locale.
[12:19] Priya: ok let's open it up for quick q&a.
[12:23] Marcus: one more — are there any hidden costs with lookahead prefetching like additional storage or egress?
[12:29] Samira: prefetch increases local memory and minor storage for persisted cache; egress is minimal as everything stays in the serving region unless you choose cross-region replication. we call out storage and memory deltas in the cost sheet.
[12:42] Lena: thanks. any operational considerations to point out?
[12:46] Jordan: monitor cache hit-rate, eviction churn, and latency tail after enabling larger prefetch windows. we recommend gradual rollouts (canary) and automatic rollback triggers if quality or latency regress beyond thresholds.
[13:00] Ethan: i'll also note that our optimizer suggests batching sizes but you can lock concurrency per route if you want stricter latency control.
[13:10] Priya: ok, i'm comfortable with the pilot. we'll be watching the quality gate closely.
[13:16] Samira: perfect — recap of next steps: we'll send the cost spreadsheet and sample scripts today; ethan will provision sandbox and ingest traces; pyxis will provide traces and confirm peering needs. schedule follow-up 9/19 to review bench.
[13:30] Lena: thanks everyone.
[13:32] Samira: thanks all — end call.

Notes on transcript quality: some product names were garbled (K-V vs KV) and a few timestamps may shift a few seconds because of recording start lag.
